definition: TAUM (Traduction Automatique à l'Université de Montréal) is the name of a research group which was set up at the Université de Montréal in 1965.
details: Most of its research was done between 1968 and 1980. It gave birth to the TAUM-73 and TAUM-METEO machine translation prototypes, using the Q-Systems programming language created by Alain Colmerauer, which were among the first attempts to perform automatic translation through linguistic analysis. The prototypes were never used in actual production. The TAUM-METEO name has been erroneously used for many years to designate the METEO System subsequently developed by John Chandioux.

explainer.lead: TAUM was a machine translation research group at the Université de Montréal founded in 1965. It matters as an early effort to perform automatic translation through linguistic analysis, producing the TAUM-73 and TAUM-METEO prototypes.

tiers.eli5: A long time ago, a group of researchers in Montreal tried to build a computer program that could translate between languages by analyzing grammar.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers study TAUM as an early example of rule-based, linguistically informed machine translation using the Q-Systems language. A pitfall is that its prototypes were never used in actual production, and the TAUM-METEO name is often confused with the later METEO System.

These were among the first attempts at automatic translation via linguistic analysis, but they were never deployed in production.

explainer.example: The TAUM-METEO prototype was designed to translate weather reports, but it was not put into operational use; the later METEO System by John Chandioux is a different project.
